Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), the biggest company in the world, is in talks to acquire Reflection AI, the creator of open-weight models. 

According to the Financial Times, talks between the two companies are still in their early stages and could take different forms. Nvidia could decide to "acqui-hire", where it would hire staff and license its technology, as it did with Groq. Such a move would help to prevent the regulatory review that the deal would attract. 

Nvidia could also decide to increase its stake in the company. It may also decide to provide it with more chips and computing power. The FT, which cited people familiar with the matter, said that the deal could be completed in the next few weeks.

A move to acquire Reflection AI would require substantial capital since the company was valued at $25 billion in the last funding round. It would be much higher than the $13 billion that Nvidia paid for Hugging Face. In addition to Nvidia, other investors in the company are Sequoia Capital,  DST Global, Lightspeed Venture, and 1789 Capital. 

A move by Nvidia to acquire Reflection would be a bet in the so-called open-source AI models that are growing in popularity. Among the most popular of these companies are from China like Moonshot, Qwen, and DeepSeek. 

Read Also: SoundHound AI Stock: Why This Nvidia-Backed AI Voice Giant Is in a Freefall

Reflection AI recently launched its first model, known as Beam, which focuses on coding and agentic performance. In the statement, the company said that the model advances Western open-weight frontier and is competitive with existing models. 

Reflection AI is burning substantial sums of money as it advances its business. It is paying SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) $150 million a month. It has also inked deals with Nebius (NASDAQ:NBIS) and Shinsegae Group. 

Nvidia, on the other hand, is betting across all areas in the AI boom. It has spent billions of dollars investing in AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Additionally, it is a big investor in neocloud companies like Nebius, CoreWeave, IREN, Lambda, Nscale. 

The company also invested in companies in optics and photonics like Coherent and Lumentum. It is also a big investor in SoundHound, Arm Holdings, and Marvell Technologies. 

Nvidia has the financial resources to make these investments. It ended the last quarter with over $99.9 billion in cash and short-term investments and is making billions of dollars in free cash flow a year.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has raised concerns about the potential dangers of advanced artificial intelligence, warning that uncontrolled development could threaten critical infrastructure and humanity.

Sanders Sounds Alarm Over AI Risks

On Saturday, in a post on X, Sanders warned that powerful technology companies were preparing for a potential AI catastrophe while continuing to develop increasingly advanced systems.

"Big Tech oligarchs are secretly preparing for a ‘catastrophic AI event’ that could threaten our banking, healthcare, internet, electricity and water systems," he wrote.

He argued that technology companies were racing to build systems they might not be able to control, raising concerns about the potential consequences for society.

"They’re racing to build a technology they can’t control and that threatens humanity," Sanders wrote.

The senator called on lawmakers to intervene, concluding his post with a direct demand: "CONGRESS MUST PAUSE ADVANCED AI DEVELOPMENT NOW."

Read Also: Anthropic's Warning Goes Beyond Pentagon Fallout as AI Giant Fears Trump Government Pressure Could Damage Customer and Partner Relationships (UPDATED)

Calls For AI Oversight

Last month, former Vice President Kamala Harris called for a slowdown in advanced AI development, urging Congress to pass AI laws, establish a federal oversight body and pursue international safety standards.

In August, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya said AI had entered a self-improvement cycle that could rapidly accelerate capabilities and drive model costs toward zero.

In June, OpenAI urged governments to establish a global body to monitor advanced AI development and coordinate slowdowns when risks outpaced safeguards.

Rival Anthropic also called for the option to pause advanced AI development to allow safety measures to keep pace with technological progress.

Burry Warned Over Big Tech’s AI Spending

Earlier this month, Investor Michael Burry said major technology companies were spending heavily on data centers because they expected to become an oligopoly too big to fail.

JPMorgan expects AI capital spending could reach $1 trillion in 2027, while Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) reportedly sought $40 billion in financing to purchase Nvidia chips.

In July, Burry also said investors had favored stronger returns over heavy AI spending, noting that Google parent Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) had underperformed the broader market since June.

He highlighted falling valuations as investors reassessed AI spending, saying, "The market has voted and the results are clear."

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) defended a proposed billionaire wealth tax, arguing that the modern economy requires new approaches to taxation as wealth increasingly concentrates among a small number of individuals.

Khanna Compares Billionaire Tax

On Saturday, in a post on X, Khanna compared California’s proposed billionaire tax with Wisconsin’s introduction of an income tax in 1911, arguing that existing tax structures must evolve alongside changes in how wealth is generated.

"In 1911, Wisconsin pioneered the income tax because a property tax on land was not sufficient when industrialization began producing most of the wealth," Khanna wrote.

He argued that California was addressing a similar challenge today, as asset appreciation allows substantial wealth to accumulate without necessarily being taxed as ordinary income.

"A billionaire tax is not class warfare or punitive, but an innovative economic solution for a changing economy," Khanna added.

Economist Highlights Billionaires’ Wealth Gains

Khanna also reshared a post from economist Gabriel Zucman, who argued that a one-time 5% wealth tax would bring Silicon Valley billionaires’ fortunes back to their Sept. 7 levels.

Zucman said their wealth was still 178% higher than on Jan. 1, 2023, despite the proposed tax.

"They’d rather let 3 million people lose their health insurance than let that happen," he wrote, criticizing opponents of the tax.

Debate Over California Billionaire Tax

Last month, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said California’s proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax could protect health coverage for 3 million residents, while accusing billionaires of spending $229 million to defeat it.

In August, Mark Cuban warned Khanna that the tax could discourage investment and push startups out of California, saying he would require companies to leave the state before investing.

Political commentator Steve Hilton also opposed the proposal, calling it an "asset-seizure tax" and warning it could drive Silicon Valley talent and investment out of the state.

Billionaire Tax Sparks Debate

Earlier, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang said he would consider paying up to $8 billion in taxes over five years a privilege if California approved the proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax.

Economist Peter Schiff, however, warned that the measure could trigger a "mass exodus" of wealthy entrepreneurs, including Mark Zuckerberg, and weaken California’s tax base by forcing billionaires to sell assets or leave the state.

In 2024, Appaloosa Management founder David Tepper said that he would remain cautious about adding to his position in Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), saying uncertainty around AI demand, earnings and future growth makes the chipmaker difficult to value. However, nearly two years later, the hedge fund holds 1.525 million Nvidia shares.

Tepper said on CNBC’s "Squawk Box" that he remains hesitant to purchase more Nvidia shares despite considering the stock attractive. He said he sold more than 80% of the fund’s Nvidia position during the second quarter. Appaloosa held roughly $85 million in Nvidia stock at the end of June 2024.

"We sold a lot of our Nvidia. We thought [the stock] was too high at the time and would come down. Unfortunately, we didn’t buy it when it came back down," Tepper said.

He questioned whether future AI models will generate enough demand and require sufficient computing power to support Nvidia’s projected expansion. "Do you have the next-generation models that can take their chip?" Tepper had asked.

Tepper also said he had little visibility into Nvidia’s earnings beyond 2025, saying he had ‘no idea’ what the picture would look like in 2026 and 2027. “I don’t believe my analysts, I don’t believe any analysts, I don’t trust myself,” he said,” Tepper said.

Referring to the conditions behind long-term growth projections, he said, “I’m not saying it won’t happen. I’m just not smart enough to know if they will."

Read Also: Nvidia Inside: Microsoft's New Laptop Runs AI Agents Without the Cloud

Tepper Boosts Nvidia, AI Infrastructure Bets

Subsequent portfolio disclosures indicate Tepper’s Nvidia caution did not amount to abandoning AI exposure. In October 2025, Tepper increased his stake by 483% with the purchase of 1.4 million shares.

By August 2026, Appaloosa Management had boosted stakes in Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE:TSM), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG), according to the latest Form 13-F. His total Nvidia holdings stood at 1,525,000 shares worth $305.1 million at the end of the quarter.

The filing also showed Appaloosa’s newest AI-related position was CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV), also backed by Nvidia, highlighting Tepper’s broader focus on infrastructure companies supporting AI development.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock remained under pressure last week, even after the company outlined its wireless ambitions. It closed the week at $162.57, down from this month’s high of $176.30. The weakness is largely due to rising credit risk, following reports that the company is seeking to borrow more money.

SpaceX Stock Pressured Despite Wireless Milestone

Space Exploration Technologies wavered after the company acquired a nationwide portfolio of licenses in the low-band spectrum. This is a major milestone because it will now become a bigger competitor to other telecom companies like AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. The deal is reportedly worth over $8 billion.

SpaceX aims to make Starlink a big name in the internet industry. This is important because it is now its biggest cash generator. In the last earnings report, the company said that Starlink generated over $4.29 billion in revenue in the second quarter and over $1.65 billion in profits. 

SpaceX faces some major challenges ahead. One of them is that it will need to deploy towers across major urban centers in the US, a process that will cost billions of dollars. At the same time, the industry is already highly competitive, with legacy carriers like AT&T and T-Mobile having a significant market share.

Read Also: Why Micron Stock is Struggling Despite Revenue Growth and a Low Valuation

SpaceX Credit Risks are Rising

Meanwhile, investors in the bond market are getting jittery about its debt. These fears jumped after the FT reported that it was seeking to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips. $10 billion of these funds will be in the form of bank loans, with the remaining amount being in investment-grade bonds.

Recent data shows that the cost to insure against SpaceX’s debt has widened recently. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps rose to 195 basis points on Friday. This means that it costs about $19,500 annually to protect $1 million of its debt against default. SpaceX’s bond yields have also continued rising. 

Analysts Expect SpaceX’s Revenue Growth to Continue

On the positive side, analysts expect SpaceX’s business to keep growing for the foreseeable future. Second-quarter revenue soared 92% to more than $7.8 billion, and analysts expect that momentum to continue in the near term.

The upcoming earnings report is expected to show that third-quarter revenue rose to $12.9 billion. Full-year revenue is projected to jump to $45 billion, driven by the company’s artificial intelligence business, which has already secured major deals with companies such as Google, Reflection AI, and Anthropic.

Analysts are also bullish on the shares, with the average price target of $219 implying a 35% upside from the current level.

The Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have held steady in recent weeks as investors have focused on rising US bond yields and the escalating situation in the Middle East. Their resilience will be tested in the coming weeks as major US companies report earnings and key economic data is released.

Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 to React to Earnings Season

The main catalyst for the US stock market this week will be the upcoming earnings season, which will kick off on Tuesday. Top US banks, including popular names like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, will release their numbers. Other non-bank companies that will release their numbers are Johnson & Johnson, UnitedHealth Group and Kinder Morgan.

Analysts are optimistic about this earnings season. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that the estimate among analysts is that earnings growth will be 29.5%. Historically, the real earnings growth tends to be 7% above the estimate. As such, there is a likelihood that the growth will be over 40%. 

The earnings growth comes at a time when American stocks are trading at discount levels. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 Index is 19.1, lower than the five and ten-year averages.

Read Also: Why Micron Stock is Struggling Despite Revenue Growth and a Low Valuation

US Consumer Inflation Report and US Bond Yields

The stock market will also react to the upcoming US consumer price index (CPI) report on Wednesday. Economists expect the data to show that the headline and core CPI numbers rose last month as gasoline and diesel prices jumped. 

The average estimate among analysts is that the headline CPI rose from 3.4% in August to 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy prices, is expected to come in at 2.5%, up slightly from the previous 2.4%.

These numbers will provide more hints about what to expect from the Federal Reserve. Economists expect the bank to leave rates unchanged in this meeting and then hike in December. 

The stock market will also react to the bond market, where the ten-year and five-year yields have pulled back in the past few days. 

Middle East Crisis

The US stock market will also react to the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, which is escalating. For example, Yemen’s Houthis launched a major attack against Saudi Arabia’s main airport, with President Donald Trump hinting that the US will intervene. 

Iran has also continued striking ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. There is also fear that the crisis will escalate. If this happens, it means that crude oil prices will continue rising in the coming weeks. This, in turn, will lead to higher inflation, pushing the Fed to hike interest rates, which may affect the stock market.

Amazon Web Services gave Decart early access to its custom Trainium3 chip in 2025, and the startup’s chip-switching capability is becoming more important as companies race to secure computing power. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent labeled Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.)an “inflationista” while releasing the “Trump Affordability Tracker” to counter her economic claims. Bessent published the data to directly contrast economic and cost-of-living metrics between the Donald Trump and Joe Biden administrations.

‘Statistical Sleight of Hand’

Bessent took to X to criticize Warren’s “Trumpflation” tracker, stating he was providing “Another day, another Econ 101 lesson for Professor Warren.” He argued her tracker “conveniently ignores the Bidenflation tidal wave that crushed American families” and “cherry-picks wage growth by refusing to acknowledge positive real wage gains” under President Trump.

He also accused her of swapping “official medical-care CPI data for premium projections when it suits her narrative.” Bessent dismissed her claims by writing, “The Harvard Square inflationista is offering a statistical sleight of hand, not a serious assessment of today’s U.S. economy.”

Read Also: Elizabeth Warren Says Trump Made '28,000+' Trades, More Than Congress Combined: ‘Stock Trading…Should Be Illegal’

The Affordability Tracker Data

To provide what he called an “apples-to-apples comparison,” Bessent shared the “Trump Tracker: The Full Picture,” updated as of Oct. 9, 2026.

The graphic reports annualized core inflation at 2.5% under Trump, compared to 4.7% under Biden. The data show cumulative real weekly wages grew 1.5% during the Trump administration, compared with a 3.9% decrease under Biden.

The document also highlights a “Record Real Median Household Income” of $87,460 and cites the “Lowest Poverty Rate in History” at 10.2%.

Employment and Living Costs

Regarding the workforce, the tracker displays an increase of 1 million private sector jobs alongside a 328,000 reduction in the federal workforce.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) President Brad Smith is pressing governments to impose urgent safety requirements on artificial intelligence.

Smith, in an interview with the BBC on Sunday, said, “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”

According to Smith, AI must be viewed as both a "tool and a weapon," arguing that governments need common rules as increasingly capable systems gain access to sensitive information and critical infrastructure. “Let’s get started today,” he said.

He proposed requiring companies to notify people affected when rogue AI agents breach systems and to submit formal reports documenting those incidents. He also supported emergency "kill switches" that could pause or slow unpredictable systems.

The Microsoft President warned that this is the time for action, citing AI agents operating beyond human control and powerful models posing cybersecurity risks. “The moment has arrived,” he said.

Smith further called for independent government evaluators to review certain AI products before launch, especially systems with capabilities that could threaten global cybersecurity.

Read Also: Microsoft's Visa Freeze Could Trigger an AI 'Brain Drain'

Smith Urges Checks Beyond AI Pledges

At the end of September, President Donald Trump hosted leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) at the White House, where they signed a "morally binding" pledge to work with independent auditors to evaluate AI systems and ensure they do not access or hack technical systems in unintended ways.

Smith welcomed the statement, saying Microsoft was "happy to sign it," but doesn’t think self-regulation alone is “sufficient any longer” because less responsible companies may not follow the same standards.

Microsoft Leaders Push for AI Safeguards

Smith’s comments come as other Microsoft-linked leaders also advocate stronger controls. Over the weekend, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said companies should treat AI models as potential insider risks and rely on external safeguards if advanced systems are compromised. Nadella said organizations cannot reliably trace model behavior to specific training data or model weights, even while granting models access to sensitive data and important actions.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates renewed the message on Sunday, calling for AI protections modeled on the safety regimes governing planes, automobiles and medicines. Gates argued that current safeguards do not adequately address AI’s risks or potential misuse.

Zuckerberg said he explained the original stream to his daughter before going live, and that she wanted to know why people found it funny.

“I think I just said smoking these meats about a hundred times,” he added.

Zuckerberg cooked on a Big Green Egg and joked that he was seeing “how much product placement” he could fit into the stream, working in Sweet Baby Ray’s barbecue sauce, actor Tom Holland’s non-alcoholic beer, and Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses.

The original October 2016 broadcast showed Zuckerberg smoking a brisket and ribs in his backyard and was later edited into viral clips.

OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming increasingly important to the broader AI trade as investors assess whether strong revenue growth can support their valuations, capital needs, and potential public listings.

OpenAI has delayed a potential IPO until 2027 after CEO Sam Altman called a 2026 listing "ill-advised," citing concerns around AI safety, governance and model alignment.

Anthropic, meanwhile, is preparing for a possible public debut as early as mid-November 2026 after confidentially filing for an IPO, with reports pointing to a potential $2 trillion valuation and a raise of up to $100 billion.

Gabelli Funds portfolio manager John Belton sees stronger financial disclosure as a positive for the market. At the same time, Tusk Ventures founder and CEO Bradley Tusk questions whether public-market pressure could create new risks.

Belton Says Revenue Growth Is Driving the AI Trade

Belton said investors are closely watching OpenAI and Anthropic because their revenue trends have helped shape sentiment across AI-related stocks.

"My view is, the sooner we get financials for those companies out in the public domain, the healthier it’s going to be for the market," Belton said.

He told CNBC last Friday that technology stocks have generally performed best when investors received evidence that revenue at OpenAI and Anthropic continued to grow.

"That has really been the story of 2026, revenue growth at those companies," Belton said.

Belton described OpenAI and Anthropic as bellwethers for generative AI and said their combined annual recurring revenue is approaching $150 billion.

He believes continued adoption and monetization of AI products can give companies confidence to keep investing in infrastructure while encouraging investors to support that spending.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Tusk Questions Public-Market Pressure

Tusk takes a more cautious view of an Anthropic IPO, particularly given CEO Dario Amodei’s focus on AI safety.

"By definition, every quarter, investors are going to be asking, ‘Where’s the growth?’" Tusk told CNBC last Friday.

He argued that pressure to meet revenue targets could encourage companies to release increasingly sophisticated models even when management has safety concerns.

Tusk said the same broader tension applies to OpenAI as both companies balance large capital requirements with pressure to grow.

Valuation Could Become a Test

Tusk raised concerns about a potential AI bubble, warning that Anthropic’s lofty valuation may be difficult to sustain without continued rapid revenue growth.

“If there is an AI bubble, and I’m pretty convinced that there is, once you really expose it, that’s when you really run the risk.”

He said Anthropic trades at roughly 27 times revenue under a generous estimate. "That’s probably not sustainable unless you’re producing continuous revenue, heading into 2027," Tusk said.

Tusk also warned that taking Anthropic public could expose its valuation to greater scrutiny and put pressure on the company to prioritize revenue growth over AI safety.

He suggested that remaining private could help shield the broader stock market from a potential correction in AI valuations, given the financial exposure of major technology companies to the sector.

He argued that Anthropic and OpenAI should focus on raising the capital they actually need at valuations they can justify rather than simply pursuing the highest possible figure.

"The goal isn’t to have a really good story on Wall Street, the goal is to ultimately have a good exit," Tusk said.

Open Models Could Add Competitive Pressure

Tusk also questioned whether most customers need the capabilities offered by the most advanced models.

He said lower-cost or free open models, including Meta Platforms Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Llama, could meet many everyday needs and potentially challenge the economic model behind ever-larger investments by Anthropic and OpenAI.

Speaking on CBS News, Sankar described the movement driving AI safety narratives as a “doomsday cult” and confirmed the military has replaced Anthropic’s models following a dispute over safeguards.

Silicon Valley Ideology vs. Economic Utility

Sankar argued that public anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence stems from theological narratives rather than technical realities. He noted that AI researchers warning of catastrophic outcomes have created a “mass psychosis” that obscures the technology’s actual impact on American enterprise and the workforce.

“There’s an unseen force driving the narrative around AI safety and it’s… this millenarian doomsday cult meets messianic complex called effective altruism,” Sankar said. “Many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine god of AGI.”

According to Sankar, tech companies carry a two-fold burden: demonstrating clear economic prosperity and taking full engineering responsibility for product safety rather than abdicating it to external researchers. Sankar noted that existing laws provide a “massive running head start” for dealing with liability.

Defense Department Operations and Model Sovereignty

Sankar stated that Anthropic’s capabilities have “already been replaced” within the system through alternative providers such as OpenAI, xAI, and open-weight models from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

“The department today has a wide range of model providers,” Sankar said. He argued that an institution’s “sovereignty and agency” relies entirely on its freedom to decide which models to use and in what context, adding: “It is your alpha.”

Responding to reports regarding a lethal strike in Minab, Sankar denied that Palantir’s AI software caused the civilian casualties. Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) executives warned Monday that financing could constrain artificial intelligence expansion, even as demand for computing infrastructure remains strong.

Capital Could Become AI’s Biggest Bottleneck

Speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said access to capital could become a bigger obstacle than shortages of chips or electricity, CNBC reported.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan also flagged rising financing costs and uncertainty over investment returns. He urged companies to improve efficiency and develop business models that deliver tangible returns.

Hock Tan expects computing demand to exceed supply through 2029, potentially extending into 2030. Intel’s CEO sees strong AI infrastructure demand over the next two to three years.

AI Borrowing Slows

The warnings follow a sharp slowdown in AI-related borrowing.

Global AI-related debt issuance fell to $23 billion in September, less than half of August’s total, the Financial Times reported, citing Morgan Stanley data covering public bonds and private placements. Monthly financing has declined since June’s $113 billion peak.

Morgan Stanley primarily attributed the slowdown to substantial borrowing earlier this year.

In June, Morgan Stanley forecast nearly $570 billion in AI-related debt issuance for 2026, Reuters reported. JPMorgan separately projected $4.1 trillion in cumulative AI debt financing through 2030.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Major Financing Deals Remain Planned

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) reportedly plans to raise $40 billion to buy NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips. Apollo Global Management, Inc. (NYSE:APO) is expected to lead the financing.

Banks are also arranging a $60 billion financing package tied to Broadcom’s chip deals with Anthropic.

Bank of America Securities analyst Tom Curcuruto estimates Broadcom’s AI financing vehicle could support about $370 billion of senior debt by mid-2029 at a 20-gigawatt scale, including roughly $150 billion of new issuance in 2027.

The structure could help Broadcom turn strong AI chip demand into actual deployments by giving customers access to outside financing for costly infrastructure.

However, Broadcom also takes on risk by backstopping some customer lease obligations. Its initial transaction exposes the company to as much as $29 billion.

Curcuruto’s estimate shows how quickly that lease-related exposure could grow as Broadcom scales the platform.

Ray Dalio and Jordi Visser agree that markets have a bubble. They disagree on where it is.

Last week, Dalio, the founder of Bridgewater Associates, described artificial intelligence as a classic bubble.

"I think we’re close to that," Dalio said of the bursting point at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore,

Visser, head of AI Macro Nexus Research at 22V Research, answered in a video published Sunday on his Youtube channel.

He said the AI bubble is not the one investors should fear.

“How many times has Ray Dalio called for a bubble over the course of since 2020? A lot,” Visser said.

Dalio’s AI Bubble Case Rests on Debt and Rates

Dalio highlighted the large amount of debt being raised to fund AI investment as the main risk for the bubble’s burst.

As interest rates climb, that debt becomes harder to carry.

The 10-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 5.24%. That is up 108 basis points, or 1.08 percentage points, since the end of 2025. The 30-year yield stood at 5.60% and the 2-year yield at 4.79%.

Dalio also said the need to turn paper wealth into cash, for example, to pay a wealth tax, could force investors to sell.

Visser Says AI Demand Still Exceeds Supply

Visser said every bubble needs supply to run ahead of demand.

That applies to speculative bubbles, capacity bubbles and credit bubbles.

In past cycles, people were the buyers. This time, he said, the buyers are AI agents.

These are software programs that carry out tasks on their own and consume computing power as they work.

"The demand side is coming from agents," Visser said. He expects their number to grow from thousands today to billions next year.

He pointed to Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE) as evidence. Chief Executive Michael Hurlston told Bloomberg Television last week that its optical components are effectively sold out through early 2029.

The stock is up 191% this year.

Valuations are his second argument.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) trades at about 20 times expected earnings for its next fiscal year. Visser said that is nowhere near dot-com multiples.

Read Also: Earnings Volatility Watch: JPMorgan, Goldman Kick Off Q3 Season, But These 10 Stocks Are Priced For Bigger Swings

The Bubble Visser Sees Is in Rate-Dependent Companies

Instead, Visser said the excess sits in older businesses that survived because borrowing costs stayed near zero for years.

"There is a bubble in companies that would have been gone a long time ago around the globe if it wasn’t for the fact that rates kept them in business," he said.

He described them as "zombie companies that grow 2 to 3% a year in revenue."

The term usually refers to a company that earns too little to cover its interest costs. It stays alive by replacing old debt with new debt.

When rates rise, each refinancing costs more.

Visser named utilities, consumer staples, household durables and autos as the most rate-sensitive areas.

What Is the Market Pricing In?

Market breadth supports part of that view.

Market breadth, the number of stocks taking part in a rally, points the same way. One common test is whether a stock trades above its 200-day moving average, the average closing price of the past 200 sessions.

Fewer than half of S&P 500 stocks currently trade above the 200-day moving average, even with the index near a record.

Only 4 of the 32 utilities in the S&P 500 pass that test. None of the four homebuilders do.

"That’s why 400 stocks go down and 100 go higher," Visser said.

Returns show the same split. The median S&P 500 stock is up 3.5% this year. Meanwhile, the index is up 13.6%.

Only two sector funds are ahead of the index.

State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLE) has gained 45.5% and State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLK) has gained 36.5%.

Polymarket traders put a 6.1% chance on an AI bubble burst in 2026, down 1.3 percentage points in a week. However, the odds rise to 18.5% for a burst by June 30, 2027.

IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN) could unlock more value from its AI data-center infrastructure after Anthropic reportedly signed a multi-year cloud contract with the company, adding another major customer to its growing computing business.

Anthropic Expands AI Capacity Through IREN

Anthropic is accelerating its data-center buildout to support rising AI demand and bring more computing capacity online.

The company has committed to more than 15 gigawatts of capacity across over 10 cloud providers, including Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) Amazon Web Services and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google, with agreements valued at about $530 billion, the Information reported on Sunday.

Anthropic expects its AI computing capacity to increase from 1.4 GW last year to 5 GW this year, 9.5 GW next year and more than 15 GW in 2028.

Faster Deployment Could Support Revenue Growth

The Information said Anthropic is moving quickly to activate new data centers because earlier deployment could generate significant additional revenue.

Investor and analyst estimates cited in the report suggest that bringing a separate 245-MW Louisiana facility online one month earlier could generate an additional $1.3 billion in sales for Anthropic.

That example highlights the potential value of quickly deploying computing infrastructure, which could support demand for providers such as IREN.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Spending And Competition Remain Risks

Anthropic’s rapid infrastructure expansion also increases its cost burden.

The Information said heavier server leasing could pressure margins, while lower spending from major customers including Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) could add further pressure.

Competition with OpenAI also remains a key factor as Anthropic continues expanding its computing footprint.

Analysts remain constructive on IREN, pointing to rising AI infrastructure demand, higher contract pricing and expanding compute capacity.

JPMorgan analyst Richard Choe recently upgraded IREN to Overweight from Underweight and raised his price forecast to $65 from $46. He expects IREN to reach about 400 MW of operational capacity by the end of 2026, supporting annual recurring revenue guidance of up to $4 billion.

Choe also said neocloud contract pricing has increased from roughly $10-$15 per watt to $15-$20 per watt or more, while customer prepayments of 25%-50% can help fund GPU purchases.

“IREN has been able to sign additional deals throughout the year at increasingly higher prices and now has a broad mix of AI customers,” Choe wrote.

BTIG analyst Gregory Lewis recently maintained a Buy rating and an $80 price forecast. He said IREN’s integrated power-and-compute model and NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) relationship support a GPU-as-a-service business running at about $4 billion annually.

Lewis expects IREN to add roughly 730 MW of compute next year and noted that the company has about 1.1 GW of international power capacity across Spain and Australia.

He expects tight power and compute supply to keep GPU rental rates firm or push them higher.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) on Monday introduced AMD Helion, an open, rack-scale computing platform designed to support agentic artificial intelligence workloads across hyperscale data centers and enterprises.

AMD Expands Agentic AI Infrastructure

Built on the company’s Helios architecture, Helion combines AMD EPYC processors, Instinct GPUs and open software to help customers optimize computing performance, power consumption and costs.

The platform offers flexible CPU and GPU configurations, including a CPU-only rack powered by sixth-generation AMD EPYC processors that supports up to 32,768 cores.

An integrated configuration combines EPYC processors and Instinct MI350P GPUs for enterprise AI workloads.

Helion also features a token router that directs AI agents’ requests across frontier and open-source models.

Industry Support and Availability

Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO), Dell Technologies Inc. (NYSE:DELL), Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (NYSE:HPE), Lenovo Group Ltd. (OTC:LNVGY), Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) and several other technology companies are supporting the platform.

AMD plans to contribute Helion’s specifications to the Open Compute Project. Partner-developed configurations are expected to become available in November 2026.

Lisa Su Sees Strong Demand Through 2027

The stock has climbed more than 200% in 2026, lifting the chipmaker’s market value above $1 trillion for the first time in September.

CEO Lisa Su recently said AMD plans to substantially increase chip supply in 2027 after expanding production capacity throughout 2026.

“We’ve been able to increase our supply as we’ve gone through 2026, and we’re going to substantially increase our supply in 2027,” Su said.

AMD is working with Foxconn, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE:TSM) and memory suppliers to secure enough production capacity to meet expected demand.

“There’s very, very high demand for the next several years. We can see very high demand, and so we need more advanced wafer capacity,” Su said.

Su said AMD is now planning capacity three to five years ahead as customers commit to larger data-center deployments.

AI Agents Could Create Another CPU Growth Driver

AMD also sees AI agents creating additional demand for traditional processors that handle data, software tools and supporting workloads.

AMD Executive Vice President Forrest Norrod said the company designed its latest EPYC processor for that opportunity.

“AI needs CPUs for tool use, and Venice CPU was designed just perfectly for that sweet spot, incredible for the next generation of data processing,” Norrod said.

AMD said Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) has deployed millions of its CPUs. Its processors are also reportedly used in AI applications including Muse and OpenAI’s Dot.

Analyst Sees Upside, but NVIDIA Raises Competition

Mizuho Securities Managing Director Jordan Klein said AMD stands to benefit as large cloud operators increase CPU spending tied to AI.

“AMD is probably getting the most of this because they have the largest market share in the cloud hyperscaler world for CPUs, best product,” Klein said.

However, Klein said NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) could intensify competition as customers already buying its GPUs consider its Vera CPU and broader data-center platform.

He also expects Meta to diversify its suppliers, with AMD, NVIDIA, Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC), Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) unit Google among potential providers.

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) went public on June 12 and, amid investor anticipation, debuted above its IPO price, surging 19% on day one. About a month later, the stock fell about 30% from its debut price. SpaceX stock has rebounded significantly over the last two months, rewarding patient investors.

SpaceX Stock Rallies

Fueled by multiple catalysts and continued strong investor demand, SpaceX stock has rallied over the last two months, helping CEO Elon Musk once again become a trillionaire.

The stock’s up-and-down price since its June 12 debut could be a good lesson in timing and patience for investors, particularly around a highly anticipated IPO.

SpaceX stock was priced at $135 for its IPO and opened trading at $150. On the first day of trading, shares were up 19%.

By the end of July, the stock price had crashed over 30% and hit a 52-week low of $104.83.

Recent launches, Musk’s optimism, and a new spectrum deal for the Starlink unit have fueled optimism in the stock price once again.

SpaceX shares closed Friday at $162.57, up 22% from their Aug. 11 close.

For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, is up only 1% over the same period: Aug. 11 to Oct. 9.

That’s a 22-to-1 outperformance for SpaceX stock over the last two months.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Top 12 Most-Searched Tickers in September on Benzinga Pro – Meta Rises, SpaceX Falls, Dell & Bloom Energy Join List

Patience Pays Off

Investors who bought in on the SpaceX IPO are up from the initial IPO price. Those who bought in on the first day of trading may be up only slightly now, at the closing price of the first day, if they chose to wait and buy shares on the first day of trading.

Others, like some members of Congress, bought SpaceX stock in the days after the market debut, when shares hit their highest levels. Those investors are holding a loss today.

The smartest investors may have been the traders who sat out the IPO entirely, waited for the dust to settle, and then bought SpaceX stock two months after the offering.

Those traders avoided periods of high volatility and are now up over 20% in two months.

With SpaceX recently securing spectrum needed for a full mobile launch and quarterly earnings expected next month, upcoming catalysts could keep the stock in the spotlight and reward the patient investors even more.

Steve Eisman warns that more than 65% of the S&P 500 is now tied to artificial intelligence, leaving investors far less diversified than they might think.

Yet the investor famous for The Big Short says he owns Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE:GEV), two major beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom.

“I own Nvidia, for example, and I watch and I worry,” he said in an interview with In the Money’s Amber Kanwar.

Suppliers Are Collecting the AI Cash

Eisman favors companies receiving AI infrastructure spending over those financing the buildout.

“I would be looking at the companies that are getting that cash flow,” he said in an interview on Oct. 8.

Nvidia supplies the chips powering data centers. Its revenue rose 106% from a year earlier to $96.2 billion in the quarter ended July 26.

GE Vernova sells gas turbines and electrical equipment needed to power AI data centers. Its companywide backlog reached $176 billion at the end of June, while data-center orders in its Electrification business topped $5 billion in the first half of 2026, more than double its full-year 2025 total.

But Eisman is taking precautions. He has partially hedged four unnamed AI-related holdings while remaining mostly long.

He worries that OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to finance their enormous commitments, potentially slowing spending throughout the supply chain.

The S&P 500’s Hidden AI Exposure

Eisman has long recommended buying the S&P 500 and leaving it alone. He now warns the index, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), provides limited protection against an AI downturn.

Information technology represents roughly 40% of the index by his count. Add Alphabet, Amazon and other technology-related companies, and the figure exceeds 50%.

Include utilities and industrial firms supplying AI infrastructure, and Eisman estimates exposure rises above 65%.

“It’s mostly all one trade. And to be perfectly frank, that makes me nervous,” he said in his podcast on Oct. 9.

The warning comes amid broader market pain. More than 40% of S&P 500 stocks have fallen in 2026, despite the index gaining roughly 14%, Reuters reported Monday.

Even bonds may offer limited shelter. Eisman estimates more than half of this year’s corporate bond issuance is AI-related, exposing lenders to the same investment cycle.

For investors seeking to avoid AI exposure, his preference is clear.

“I would just buy short-term treasuries,” he said.

On Polymarket, traders assign approximately 6% odds to a qualifying AI industry downturn by year-end. The contract requires at least three specified stress events within a 90-day period, rather than an ordinary market correction.

Eisman isn’t predicting a collapse, and he’s still long Nvidia and GE Vernova.

Bitmine Immersion Technologies (NYSE:BMNR) bought 12,532 more Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) last week, inching closer to Chairman Tom Lee‘s 5% supply cap that will trigger a full stop on purchases.

Holdings Near the Finish Line

Bitmine announced Monday that its crypto holdings, cash and marketable securities now total $16.2 billion. 

As of Oct. 11, the company held 6,028,946 ETH, worth $2,544 per token, equal to 4.9% of the total 122.1 million ETH supply.

As Benzinga reported last week, Lee said at Token2049 that Bitmine will stop buying once it reaches 5%, needing only about 100,000 more ETH to get there. 

At last week’s pace, that puts the company roughly six to seven weeks from hitting its target.

Why Lee Calls This the Start of a Bigger Bull Run

Bitmine released its October Chairman’s Message on Oct. 7, titled “Crypto Bull Underway—This Cycle Likely the Largest.” 

Lee pointed to four forces he expects to drive the next cycle: tokenization, wealth transfer, digital asset treasuries absorbing supply, and crypto’s role as a downstream AI story.

On wealth transfer specifically, Lee cited Robinhood (NASDAQ:HOOD) CEO Vlad Tenev’s recent comment that $100 trillion in wealth is changing hands, with IRS and Fundstrat data estimating $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion of that shifting between 2026 and 2028. 

Moreover, Lee argued younger heirs tend to carry higher risk appetite for crypto, making this wealth transfer a stronger tailwind than the one seen in the 2019-2021 cycle.

He also flagged digital asset treasuries like Bitmine as a structural difference from prior cycles, since these companies remove supply from circulation permanently rather than trading it.

BMNP Preferred Stock Outperforms Comparable Yields

Bitmine’s preferred stock, BMNP (NYSE:BMNP), issued at $80 in June, has gained 24% since launch and last closed at $99.53. 

Lee said BMNP’s 9.56% yield sits 256 basis points below Strategy’s (NASDAQ:MSTR) comparable Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) credit yield and 515 basis points below Solana’s (CRYPTO: SOL) CHAD yield, which he called evidence of ETH’s stronger yield and stability profile.

ETH’s Quarterly Performance Against Stocks

Lee also highlighted that ETH outperformed the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) by 6,832 basis points in the third quarter, despite a hawkish Fed, rising oil prices, and tightening global financial conditions.

BMNR stock also outperformed ETH itself during the 2025-2026 bear market, falling just 3% over the first nine months of 2026 compared to ETH’s 10% decline.

Where BMNR Stands Technically

BMNR is consolidating after pulling back from September’s $29 high.

The final four months of the year are a particularly interesting period for stock markets, often associated with recognizable seasonal patterns.

In this article, we’ll analyze market performance in September, October, November, and December, comparing two major stock indexes: the S&P 500 for the U.S. market and the DAX as a European benchmark.

Our goal is to determine whether the final four months of the year have historically shown recurring patterns and whether those patterns have been similar or different across the two markets. We’ll also examine fourth-quarter returns following a positive or negative September.

S&P 500 and DAX: Comparing US and European Stock Markets

To represent the two markets, we selected the S&P 500 for the United States and the DAX for Europe. The S&P 500 includes 500 leading U.S. companies and covers a substantial share of U.S. stock market capitalization, making it one of the most widely used benchmarks for U.S. equity performance.

The DAX, meanwhile, includes 40 leading German-listed companies and represents one of Europe’s most important stock markets. It’s worth emphasizing that the DAX specifically represents the German market, rather than Europe as a whole. Nevertheless, its size and significance make it a useful benchmark for comparing a major European stock market with its U.S. counterpart.

The two indexes also differ in their sector composition. At current weights, technology plays a particularly prominent role in the S&P 500, while industrials account for the largest share of the DAX, followed by financial services.

These weights are a snapshot of the indexes’ current composition and should not be treated as constant over time. Sector exposure has shifted over the years, as have the companies included in each index and their relative weights.

September Through December: What Average Returns Show

Let’s start by examining the average return for each of the final four months of the year, using data beginning in 1998. As Figure 1 shows, September is the only one of these months with a negative average return in both markets: approximately -1.06% for the DAX and -0.62% for the S&P 500.

The picture changes considerably in October, which posts an average positive return of approximately 1.55% for the DAX and 1.18% for the S&P 500. The two markets show even more similar results in November, with average returns of 1.54% and 1.50%, respectively.

December also shows positive average returns, although the gap between the two indexes is wider: the DAX averages approximately 1.45%, while the S&P 500 averages 0.68%.

Overall, Figure 1 reveals a broadly similar seasonal pattern across the U.S. and German markets.

Figure 1. Average monthly returns for the DAX and S&P 500 from September through December, based on the sample beginning in 1998.

A Long Strategy From October to January

The initial analysis shows that both the S&P 500 and the DAX have historically posted positive average returns in each of the final three months of the year. Based on this finding, we can construct a very simple strategy: open a long position at the beginning of October and hold it until the beginning of January.

We can then introduce another variable. As we’ve seen, September is the only month in the final four months of the year with a negative average return in both markets. We therefore divided the trades into two groups: those following a positive September and those following a negative September. This allows us to examine whether the previous month’s performance is associated with differences in returns over the following three months.

Average Q4 Returns Are Higher After a Negative September

Looking at Figure 2, the first notable feature is the strong similarity between the equity curves of the strategies applied to the DAX and the S&P 500. The curves follow broadly similar paths over time, further highlighting similarities in the seasonal patterns observed in the two markets.

It’s also important to remember that these strategies are deliberately simple and include no risk management rules. Positions are opened at the beginning of October and held until January, regardless of what happens in between. This is particularly evident in 2008, when the sharp stock market decline caused a significant drawdown in the equity curves.

The most interesting finding, however, concerns performance following September. Although the number of trades is nearly identical in the two groups, the strategies that enter the market after a negative September show substantially higher average returns. For the DAX, the average return per October-to-January trade rises from approximately 3.73% after a positive September to 5.80% after a negative September. A similar pattern emerges in the S&P 500, where the average return increases from approximately 2.37% to 4.63%.

In both markets, September weakness does not necessarily persist into the following months. On the contrary, within the sample analyzed, the final three months of the year delivered better average results when September had ended in negative territory.

Figure 2. Equity curves for the October-to-January long strategy on the DAX and S&P 500, separating trades following a positive September (dashed lines) from those following a negative September (solid lines).

From Seasonality to a Trading Strategy: Limitations and Further Research

The analysis of the final four months of the year reveals broadly similar seasonal patterns in the S&P 500 and the DAX. An even more interesting finding emerges when September’s performance is introduced as a filter: for both indexes, the average October-to-January return was substantially higher following a negative September.

One possible explanation is mean reversion, or a recovery following a decline. If the conditions behind the selloff do not develop into a deeper crisis, some of that decline may subsequently be reversed.

Once again, the analysis presented here should primarily be viewed as a starting point for further research. The simple strategy used does not include stop losses, early exit criteria, or other forms of risk management. The pattern could be explored further by introducing filters based on the size of September’s decline, the longer-term trend, or different entry and exit rules.

Until next time, happy trading!

Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) stock is under pressure Monday after a company contractor pleaded guilty to helping illegally export servers with advanced Nvidia Corp. What Sun Admitted in Court

Sun pleaded guilty to four charges: conspiring to violate U.S. export controls, smuggling, defrauding the U.S. government and obstructing justice.

It describes Sun as a broker and fixer who helped set up fake servers in December 2025 and lied to a U.S. Department of Commerce official during an inspection. According to the indictment, the servers had already been diverted to China.

Co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and Taiwan sales manager Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang were also indicted.

The U.S. restricts sales of advanced AI chips to China on national security grounds. According to the indictment, the restrictions cover Nvidia’s B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, as well as servers equipped with these chips.

California-based Super Micro said it terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year.

In a Sunday Substack post, hedge fund manager Michael Burry said almost all of his short exposure now consists of put options on two instruments: the Nasdaq-100 Index and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH).

His Nasdaq-100 puts expire in April 2027, while his SMH puts expire in June 2027. Both positions are roughly 20% out of the money, according to his post.

Burry said he believes the market is within zero to nine months of a significant top, arguing that the final stages of the bull market could become volatile as major indexes reach new highs.

Read Also: Michael Burry Warns Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Could Become ‘Worthless’ as Trump-Era Gains Collapse Under Fresh Pressure

SMH is Central to Burry’s Thesis

Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) accounts for 19.6% of SMH, followed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) at 9.3% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) at 5.6%. Together, the three stocks represent 34.5% of the portfolio. Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO), Micron Technology, Inc (NASDAQ:MU), Marvell Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MRVL) and Applied Materials Inc (NASDAQ:AMAT) each account for around 5%.

That concentration makes SMH particularly sensitive to changes in semiconductor demand, AI infrastructure spending and investor expectations for future earnings.

A slowdown in hyperscaler capital expenditure or disappointment in chipmakers’ growth forecasts could pressure the ETF. Conversely, sustained AI investment and strong earnings could undermine Burry’s bearish position.

4 Other ETFs to Watch as Burry’s Warning Unfolds

These ETFs offer different ways to assess semiconductor and broader technology exposure.

  • Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ): Tracks the Nasdaq-100, making it a broader gauge of large-cap growth stocks that could face pressure if investors rotate away from expensive technology shares.
  • iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX): Provides a comparison with SMH. SOXX returned 79% year to date, underscoring the scale of the semiconductor rally that Burry is challenging.
  • ProShares Short QQQ (NYSE:PSQ): Seeks daily returns that are the inverse of the Nasdaq-100’s performance, offering a bearish alternative without directly purchasing put options. Its daily objective makes it unsuitable as a straightforward long-term substitute for Burry’s trade.
  • Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bear 3X Shares (NYSE:SOXS): Offers a more aggressive alternative to Burry’s bet. The ETF targets three times the inverse of its semiconductor benchmark’s daily performance, amplifying gains during a sector downturn but magnifying losses if chip stocks rally. Unlike Burry’s long-dated SMH put options, SOXS resets daily, making it primarily a short-term trading instrument rather than a direct replica of his strategy.

Whether Burry’s market-top warning proves right remains to be seen, but his shift toward Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor puts puts the AI trade’s biggest winners under scrutiny.

Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) CEO Hock Tan warned Monday that many artificial intelligence investors don’t understand what they’re buying, comparing their behavior to casino gambling even as his company forecasts $230 billion in annual AI chip revenue by fiscal 2028.

“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” Tan said at an event in Singapore, Bloomberg reported.

He said investors were setting “very extreme expectations,” only to discover that investing in AI was “almost like they are in a casino.”

Tan also questioned whether businesses were getting value from AI, comparing companies experimenting with the technology to children burning through arcade tokens without learning anything.

Tan’s concerns extended to the companies supplying those AI services.

He said OpenAI’s roughly $50 billion annualized revenue in September demonstrated strong demand, but its enormous training costs offered little indication of long-term profitability.

Broadcom’s $230 Billion AI Bet

Tan’s warning comes as Broadcom enjoys extraordinary growth from the AI investment boom.

The company reported $16.7 billion in fiscal third-quarter AI semiconductor revenue, up 221% year over year, and expects $21.7 billion in the fourth quarter.

Broadcom develops custom AI chips and networking equipment for data centers, with OpenAI and Anthropic among the customers underpinning its growth expectations.

Tan forecasts annual AI chip revenue will quadruple from approximately $58 billion this fiscal year to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.

Part of that projected growth depends on OpenAI, whose long-term profitability Tan himself questions.

Capital Could Become the Next AI Bottleneck

Tan warned that access to financing, rather than memory chip shortages, could become the industry’s biggest constraint.

Broadcom itself is increasingly involved in financing the expansion.

Banks last week began syndicating a $60 billion AI financing package tied to Anthropic’s lease of Google-designed chips, including $42 billion in senior loans supported by Broadcom’s credit rating, the Financial Times reported.

The arrangement could help turn demand for AI chips into actual sales, while exposing Broadcom to additional financial risks if customers struggle to meet their commitments.

On Polymarket, traders assign a 6% probability to a qualifying AI downturn by December 31, with $2.44 million traded. The contract requires three of six events within 90 days, including 50% declines from record highs for Broadcom or Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Broadcom shares fell 1% to $357 in late-morning trading Monday, leaving the stock roughly 28% below its 52-week high of $495.
